finding.claim: Public-key certificate auth verifies only the certificate's signature and validity window. It never checks cert_type == User or that the requested username is in valid_principals before calling handler.auth_openssh_certificate. A host certificate, or a certificate for another principal, signed by a CA the application trusts can authenticate as any user the handler accepts.
finding.source: SSH publickey userauth request carrying a *-cert-v01@openssh.com certificate blob (attacker-controlled bytes from the network).
finding.sink: handler.auth_openssh_certificate(user, cert) at russh/src/server/encrypted.rs:782, which grants login when the application returns Accept.

trace.note: PublicKeyOrCertificate::decode parses the attacker-supplied cert blob.
cert.verify_signature() checks only that the embedded CA signed the cert; no cert_type or principal check follows.
Certificate public key is used as the pubkey for the signature check.
Signature verification of the userauth request with the certificate's key.
Certificate passed to the application handler, which alone decides acceptance.
Default auth_openssh_certificate rejects, so exposure requires the application to override it and trust the CA.

finding.guards_checked: Validity window (encrypted.rs:702-711) and certificate signature (encrypted.rs:714) are enforced. The library performs no cert_type check and no valid_principals-vs-user check anywhere in src/server (grep found none). The default handler rejects (server/mod.rs:291-296). Not verified: whether ssh-key's verify_signature performs any extra checks, because the crate source is not in the local cargo registry.

finding.claim: check_known_hosts_path returns Ok(false), meaning unknown, when a recorded key has a different algorithm from the presented key. Only same-algorithm mismatches return KeyChanged. A caller that learns and accepts on Ok(false) lets a MITM replace a host's key with one of a different type without a warning.
finding.source: Host key of a different algorithm presented by the server during the handshake (network-controlled).
finding.sink: Caller's host-key acceptance policy, driven by the Ok(false) return at known_hosts.rs:48.

trace.note: Match on (algorithm equal, key equal); the (false, _) arm yields Ok(false).
KeyChanged is returned only for the (true, false) arm, i.e. same algorithm.
Ok(false) is returned to the caller, indistinguishable from no entry.

finding.guards_checked: Same-algorithm key change is detected (known_hosts.rs:38). Exact host and hashed host matching is in place. Practical exploitability depends on the caller treating Ok(false) as accept-and-learn. OpenSSH behaves similarly, so this is an API-clarity risk rather than a library bypass.

finding.claim: known_host_keys_path ignores @revoked marker lines. A revoked key is therefore not rejected and reads as unknown, which is exploitable only if the caller accepts unknown keys.
finding.source: A user-maintained known_hosts file containing an @revoked entry for a host (local configuration, plus the server-presented key).
finding.sink: check_known_hosts_path result at known_hosts.rs:48, consumed by the caller's host-key policy.

trace.note: Line split on spaces; the first field is the marker or host pattern.
match_hostname compares the host against the marker, so @revoked lines never match and are skipped.
Result is Ok(false) for a revoked key, the same as an unknown key.

finding.guards_checked: Ordinary host lines are matched. There is no @revoked handling anywhere in src. Impact depends on the caller's policy for unknown keys.
